title: Interregional Absorptive Reserve Sizing — Notes and Tactical Plan
body:
Purpose:

This note captures a lightweight, operational approach for sizing an "absorptive reserve" — the spare GPU capacity we intentionally hold in neighboring regions to absorb transient and regional-failure demand spikes without degrading customer SLAs. Unlike long-term cold standby, the absorptive reserve is distributed, modest in size per-region, and designed to be pulled into service automatically by smart routing and ephemeral burst pools.

Goals:
- Define assumptions and formulas for absorptive reserve sizing for Q1–Q3 2027 planning.
- Produce 3 scenario buckets (normal churn, region-degraded, major loss) with concrete reserve % targets per region.
- Provide a runbook for quick activation, monitoring thresholds, and rollback criteria.
- List telemetry and experiments needed to validate the model before committing capacity.

Context and motivation:
Redwood’s serving runtime and smart routing allow us to route overflow to alternate regions with minimal code changes. We saw two spikes in 2026 where customer-facing latencies rose due to bursty peaks and a short regional availability zone outage. Holding all spare capacity in a single cold pool is expensive and slow to scale. The absorptive reserve is intended to be: distributed, used for short-term absorption (minutes-to-hours), and automatically reclaimed when normal routing resumes.

Key definitions (for this doc):
- Absorptive Reserve (AR): spare usable GPU vcores / nodes in a secondary region kept in warm state with preloaded common model artifacts to shorten cold-starts.
- Absorption Event: any episode where primary-region throughput exceeds provisioned capacity or suffers partial outage and traffic is routed to AR.
- Absorptive Efficiency: % of overflow traffic served by AR without exceeding target p99 latency SLO.

Assumptions (base):
- Baseline per-region 95th percentile sustained utilization target (for production pools): 60%
- Burst safety threshold (when AR is considered): 75% sustained for 3 consecutive minutes
- Typical request distribution across regions: NA 52%, EU 30%, APAC 18% (by token volume)
- Cold-start penalty for full cold pool spin-up: ~120–180s; warm AR target to be <= 30s for first-response latency
- Model mix: 45% medium (7–13B), 40% large (30–70B quantized), 15% embeddings/high-IO workloads

Sizing heuristic (starter formula):
We want AR_size(region) = max(MinimumReserve, floor( alpha * steady_demand(region) + beta * regional_risk_factor ))
Where:
- steady_demand(region) = average GPU demand over last 30d (normalized to GPU-equivalent units)
- alpha = burst cushion coefficient (recommended 0.20 => cover 20% of steady demand)
- beta = risk multiplier tied to latency exposure and critical customers (recommended 0.05–0.15 of steady demand)
- MinimumReserve = 2 GPU-equivalent units for small regions to ensure headroom for routing and tests

Concrete initial parameters we will test: alpha=0.20, beta=0.10, MinimumReserve=2.
Examples (rounded):
- NA steady_demand = 1200 GPU-units => AR_NA = floor(0.20*1200 + 0.10*1200) = floor(240 + 120) = 360 units (~30 nodes of A10x or equivalent)
- EU steady_demand = 700 => AR_EU = floor(0.20*700 + 0.10*700) = 210 units
- APAC steady_demand = 400 => AR_APAC = 120 units

Scenario buckets and target absorbable fraction:
- Routine burst (5–10x short tail): aim to absorb 30–40% of overflow with AR; latency degradation tolerated up to +10% p99 for < 15 minutes.
- Degraded region (partial AZ outage): absorb 60–80% of overflow for 30–120 minutes while routing/stateful failovers execute.
- Major region loss (complete region down): AR is NOT intended to fully replace a region. Target absorbable fraction <= 25% of full region capacity for < 6 hours; enterprise escalation to reserved capacity / customer-specific failover policies.

Operational design and placement:
- Distribute AR across at least two adjacent regions for each primary region (e.g., NA-east backed by NA-west + EU as cross-continental fallback in extreme scenarios).
- Warm VM images with preloaded model artifacts, common quantization files, and cached KV slices for top 10% of model prompts to reduce first-token latency.
- Keep AR in a warm state (hot networking, but lower scheduler priority) to minimize cost while remaining responsive.

Routing & admission control behavior (high level):
1) Detect overflow: Composite signal = (queue length > Q_threshold) OR (node_utilization > 75% for 3m) OR (latency SLO breaches x2).
2) Local autoscaler kicks immediate short-lived burst VMs (fast path) up to local spare capacity.
3) If local capacity exhausted, routing policy adds AR regions based on latency/cost preference with weighted routing to maintain SLO.
4) Admission controller applies per-customer QoS to protect enterprise reservations (dedicated capacity) from noisy neighbors.

Monitoring and SLO thresholds to trigger AR actions:
- Primary triggers: region_utilization_5m > 75% AND p99_latency_5m > baseline_p99 * 1.10
- Soft triggers: queue_depth_1m > 250 requests, error_rate_1m > 0.5%
- Backoff criteria: primary_region_utilization drops < 65% for 10m and p99_latency returns to baseline for 5m

Cost/ROI considerations (back-of-envelope):
- Warm AR has ~30–45% lower hourly cost than fully dedicated idle pools due to lower CPU allocation and prioritized cold-launch resource sharing.
- Using AR to shave peak bursts can reduce on-demand spin-up costs by 40–60% vs naive horizontal scaling across cloud zones during short spikes.
- We need an experiment to quantify customer-perceived quality degradation for AR-served requests (A/B test on a subset of non-critical workloads).

Experimentation plan (before committing capacity):
1) Synthetic spike replay: re-run two 2026 incidents with our routing simulation and measure expected AR utilization and p99s.
2) Canary live test: enable AR routing for 5% of traffic from a non-critical tenant group for 2 weeks. Collect p50/p95/p99 and error rates.
3) Cost simulation: compare hourly bill of AR model (warm) vs incremental on-demand spin-ups using cloud pricing models and our historical autoscale logs.

Activation runbook (concise steps):
- T0 (detect): Automated alert posted to infra-alerts Slack + SRE oncall. Dashboard auto-highlights region-overflow chart.
- T+1m: Local autoscaler attempts to scale. If after +2m still above thresholds, controller runs AR-route_plan and begins traffic redirect.
- T+3–5m: AR warm instances accept traffic. SRE monitors AR_efficiency and p99 metrics.
- T+15m: If AR_efficiency < 40% and p99 degraded > 20% from baseline, abort AR and escalate to leadership + product owner (possible customer communications).
- Recovery: When primary returns to acceptable utilization and latency, gradually drain AR (scale-down policy over 10–30 minutes) and run post-mortem.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Model artifact mismatch: ensure AR image versions are on a frequent sync schedule; fail safe is to route to smaller quantized model variant rather than a mismatched large model.
- AR network congestion: prefer geographically closer AR regions and enforce network egress limits; add network-aware routing weight.
- Noisy neighbor / QoS bleed: use per-tenant admission control; enforce priority queueing for enterprise reserved traffic.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Beta reserve percent: stick to alpha=0.20 or a more conservative 0.30 for Q1? (Recommend start at 0.20 and iterate after canary.)
- Cost cap policy: set a monthly spend ceiling for global AR usage before manual approval? (Yes — propose $X/month, TBD by finance.)
- Cross-region data residency impacts: some customers may not allow processing outside a region — need product gating to prevent AR routing for those orgs.

Next steps (owner & timeline):
- 2026-11-16: Simulation runs (owner: Diego Morales) — feed with last 180d traffic profile.
- 2026-11-20: Canary config and safety policy drafted (owner: Rina Shah).
- 2026-11-30: Run canary for 2 weeks and compile metrics (owner: SRE oncall + Product).
- December Q1 planning: propose committed AR sizing in the infra budget if canary looks good.

Appendix A — Quick calc helpers (text friendly):
- Convert model mix to GPU-equivalent: GPUs_needed = sum_over_models( token_throughput_model / model_throughput_per_gpu ). Use 95th throughput for buffer.
- Warm-hours cost estimate = AR_units * warm_hourly_rate * expected_trigger_hours_per_month.

Appendix B — Minimal dashboard items:
- Region utilization (1m/5m/15m), queue depth, p50/p95/p99, AR_utilization, AR_first_token_latency, per-tenant throttling events, cost burn-rate per-hour.

Notes / quick links: see linked artifacts for related proposals and open tickets. This doc is a working draft; please comment inline with simulation results or alternative alpha/beta suggestions.
